stories.title_en: Old Bitly Links Are Being Hijacked

comments.author: xp84
comments.text:
Link shorteners
that are outsourced
are in my humble opinion an order of magnitude worse for the internet than they would be if in-house.
The way they accrete URLs over time, and then time passes, and anything can happen (your account gets deactivated, shortener company goes out of business / experiences catastrophic data loss / etc) is just asking for permanently broken links which may be unfixable.
Especially when you consider how these services can, unless they're spammy enough to inject gross interstitial ad pages, make 0 revenue from you if you aren't currently paying for a premium service, it's easy to see how they can go under.
Note: Clearly with the kind of ephemeral crap these 2011 tweets were, I'm assuming the 'attacker' publicized "Hey guys look at these funny tweets" because obviously who cares about 15 year old McDonalds marketing messages. But in general it's sad to see these still being used. To be fair to bitly, they do offer the ability to use your own domain at least, but sadly, with a service targeted mainly at marketing departments, usually they don't have the ability to work with the in-house tech team(s) to even set up DNS.

comments.author: Alive-in-2025
comments.text:
There's a lot of abandoned url ownership things on the internet. We need something like a bureau that keeps track of what it was for. We do have archive.is or .org to save the content at a url (side note - are these archivers legal or in some country that allows this?).
I do often come across an article occasionally where someone is writing about a narrow topic that I'm interesting in, but I can't find them any more - maybe they had a vauge user name that isn't resolvable.
You have sites trying to block spammers, but you have over-active groups like Reddit that seem to delete accounts aggressively with no information about what you did wrong. I want a meta id that I own, that people can check I'm the real "foo-bar1418", and that can't be deleted or taken over.
It feels like there's still room for a super-crosssite-ID. But there are also spammers, haters etc that sites have to deal with.

comments.author: g-b-r
comments.text:
Somewhat related, I've been getting a lot of spam with links to urls of big, reputable, organizations, such as universities.
You'd think that the organization was hacked, but in all these case instead these were old domains that used CNAMEs.
The domain that the CNAME pointed to was once owned and used by the organization, but at some point it was let go, and it ended up being purchased by the spammers.
So, the spammers were able to use links that looked safe, and maybe that also helped with passing spam filters.
Thus, if you manage domains, please keep track of the ones with CNAMEs, recommend the users to tell you when they stop using them, and maybe check every once in a while (better if automatically) that the domain they're pointing to hasn't changed hands.
I'd be curious to know how the spammers find these old cname domains, by the way.

comments.author: Animats
comments.text:
Intelligence has evolved on Earth at least three times - mammals, corvids, and octopuses. All the mammals have roughly the same brain architecture. But the corvids are not on the same evolutionary branch, and have a different neuron design and a different brain architecture. "Such behavioral flexibility might seem unexpected
because a layered cerebral cortex, the highest integration
center in the mammalian brain, is not existant in birds."[1] So there's more than one way to do intelligence. Useful to know for AI purposes.
Octopuses have a much more distributed system than mammals, suggesting a quite different approach is possible.

comments.author: Velocifyer
comments.text:
I'm glad that this is bringing attention to flicker sensitivity.
Here are some other things that people are sensitive to:
- CRI on white LEDs (and flourencents).
CRI is how clean the spectrum is in comparison to the sun or a incandescent bulb, where the specturm is completely even. There are some CRI >=95 LEDs that are fine for most people however.
- Motion blur
Motion blur on LCDs (such as ~50% of Nintendo Switch 2s) can hurt eyes trying to keep track of what is going on.

comments.author: explosion-s
comments.text:

Even more interestingly it’s essentially only screens— backlist posters at the mall (paper with a backlight) still affect it but less so. To me perhaps it’s focusing on something on a screen that does this, but it’s really interesting to see this affect the general population.
It’s also odd to think about lack of ability to concentrate, and I wonder if screens cause this optically somehow but to a less noticeable degree even when less intense than this new one? (Independent distracting contents)
I noticed that adding a severe red filter to all my screens helped me significantly with the concussion and am also curious about that, would that impact the intensity of a refresh perhaps? Is blue light specifically the problem? I’m unsure but have a plethora of subjective experience.
I’m glad for this to enter public consciousness a bit and would love to see more research on the screen itself impacting our brain.

This article is only about understanding the implementation of positional embeddings, but to really understand positional embeddings you have to understand the theory. Positional embeddings are group representations. This is how you find them, and this is also how you parameterize them to make them differentiable/learnable. To give a few examples:

And if you only operate locally, you can use a local bank to process credit cards...assuming you meet normal criteria -- if you don't meet normal criteria, it's reasonable for Stripe to decline your credit card processing business.
So my advice, if you want to operate locally work with a local banker, a local lawyer, and a local insurance agent. These might not scale, but scaling is only a problem once you have a going business. Good luck.

comments.author: waximabbax
comments.text:
By this logic, shouldn't any code using an open-source framework or language also be open source? Even before AI, devs learned from Stack Overflow and plenty of open source code.
You're confusing writing code with software engineering. Devs never just wrote code, they took ownership of the outcome. Business owners put their money on the line for product decisions.
To say that just because devs or founders use AI to write code, the code is no longer their intellectual property is ridiculous. Humans take responsibility for the outcome and are willing to accept the losses. AI can't do that. AI doesn't have any stakes in the output it generates, humans do.

comments.author: decoding
comments.text:
My two cents. I'm on both sides of this (as I'm sure many here are): AI was trained on my open-source code. Also I use AI to build proprietary code.
My stance is that AI is a tool, like a compiler is a tool. AI generated code should not be considered public domain or forced to be open source or ineligible for copyright.
Even if AI writes every line, the direction and engineering that I put in has been substantial (current project in mind), months of heavy AI use for heavy refinement and direction of complex software. That human input, even if it isn't lines of code, counts for a lot.
Furthermore, what does society gain from my code being made open source if anybody else could just themselves go to Claude Code and ask for the same thing?  Just go have Claude make one for you.  Is it the token cost barrier?  That is IMHO negligible compared to the value that we are getting out of AI right now.  We are in a golden moment, anybody can create amazing things, rapidly, at low cost and little barrier to entry.

comments.author: blagie
comments.text:
I am the author of multiple AGPL systems, many in mainstream use. Early LLM models would spit out my code almost verbatim. Modern systems borrow heavily on the creative design of those systems.
One company first pirated my AGPL code (e.g. shipped it without my name, copyright notices, source availability, etc.). I sent them violation notices. After many months of fighting, they had an LLM clone the system. The LLM clone feels:
a) Buggy and bad compared to my code
b) Still, like it's basically my creative content
It's as if you asked an LLM to rewrite Harry Potter, with the same plot, but bad dialogue.

comments.author: viraptor
comments.text:
Doe v. GitHub already decided (I'm simplifying, read the actual thing yourself) that LLM output is not automatically open source - or specifically it doesn't infringe on the open source training material and doesn't inherit the oss copyright notice.
Thaler v. Perlmutter (again simplified) showed 100% AI output can't be given any copyright.
The directions the current cases are going are very much opposed to that idea and I wouldn't expect things to change in the opposite direction.

comments.author: glitchc
comments.text:
The article contradicts itself.
It's important to remember that the purpose of the license is to allow the copyright owner to exercise their rights in a manner they deem fit. Even if they choose to give the code away, that choice is captured in the form of a specifically worded license (MIT, BSD, etc.).
This means that licenses exist because code is copyrightable in the first place, with the license governing the use of said copyright. If AI code is not copyrightable, then no license can govern it.

comments.author: semiquaver
comments.text:
I really have to wonder what context this person is operating in. The vast majority of software written in the world is proprietary, written for a company to aid some business process, and ridiculously specific to its use case, and freely intermixed with proprietary business information.
“Open sourcing” is not just a legal state, it’s an affirmative act that takes work to prepare the codebase for public consumption. Saying that all the weird business code in the world should be involuntarily publicized is an incoherent concept. What precisely would OP expect to happen in a world that adhered to their opinion? Because to be clear, 90%+ of all code being written today is LLM-generated, so OP suggests that companies should no longer have any privacy wrt their internal software, all LLM code just gets yeeted into the public. How could that
possibly
work?
Given how easy it is to write software now, this perspective seems to overindex on a past state of the world that no longer applies.
